sections.title: Why Go for Data Structures and Algorithms

content.text: Go is an excellent choice for Data Structures and Algorithms problems and coding interviews. Its simplicity, fast compilation, and powerful standard library make it ideal for solving algorithmic challenges efficiently.
Advantages of Go

items.label: Fast Compilation
items.description: Instant feedback loop when testing solutions. No waiting for builds.

items.label: Simple Syntax
items.description: Less boilerplate than Java or C++. Focus on the algorithm, not the language.

items.label: Strong Typing
items.description: Catch errors at compile time. Fewer runtime surprises.

items.label: Built-in Concurrency
items.description: Goroutines and channels for parallel algorithms when needed.

items.label: Efficient Memory
items.description: Value semantics by default. Control over memory layout.

items.label: Great Standard Library
items.description: sort, heap, container packages cover most algorithm needs.

content.text: Go vs Other Languages for Interviews

While Python is popular for its brevity and Java for its ubiquity, Go offers a sweet spot: it's expressive enough for quick solutions but gives you control when you need it. Most interviewers are comfortable with Go, and companies like Google, Uber, and Dropbox actively use it.

content.title: Interview Tip
content.message: When interviewing, mention that you chose Go for its clarity and performance. Interviewers appreciate candidates who can articulate their language choice.

content.message: Don't use pointers unnecessarily. Slices and maps already contain internal pointers to their data, so modifications inside functions affect the original. Use pointers mainly for tree/graph nodes and when you need nil semantics.

content.text: Many algorithm problems require you to print output instead of returning values. Go's fmt package provides powerful printing functions. Understanding format verbs and output patterns is essential for competitive programming and coding interviews where output format matters.
The Three Basic Print Functions
Go provides three main printing functions, each with a different purpose. Understanding when to use each one will save you debugging time.

items.label: fmt.Println
items.description: Adds spaces between all arguments, adds newline at end. Best for quick debugging.

items.label: fmt.Print
items.description: No newline. Adds spaces between non-string arguments only. Use for precise control.

items.label: fmt.Printf
items.description: Formatted output with placeholders. Use when format matters (interviews, competitive).

content.text: What Are Format Verbs?

Format verbs are special placeholders that start with the percent sign (%). When you use Printf, each % placeholder gets replaced by the corresponding argument. Think of them as "fill in the blank" markers that tell Go how to convert a value into text.
The 5 Most Important Format Verbs
You'll use these five verbs in 90% of your code. Master these first, and you can handle almost any printing task.

items.label: %d
items.description: Decimal integer. Use for any whole number (int, int64, etc.). The 'd' stands for 'decimal' (base 10).

items.label: %s
items.description: String. Use for string values. The 's' stands for 'string'.

items.label: %f
items.description: Float. Use for decimal numbers (float32, float64). The 'f' stands for 'floating point'.

items.label: %t
items.description: Boolean (true/false). The 't' stands for 'truth value'.

items.label: %v
items.description: Value (any type). Go figures out the best format automatically. The 'v' stands for 'value'. This is your go-to for debugging!

content.code:
// %d - Decimal integer (most common for numbers)
count := 42
fmt.Printf("Count: %d\n", count)        // Count: 42
fmt.Printf("Negative: %d\n", -17)       // Negative: -17

// %s - String (for text)
name := "Bob"
fmt.Printf("Hello, %s!\n", name)        // Hello, Bob!

// %f - Float (for decimal numbers)
price := 19.99
fmt.Printf("Price: %f\n", price)        // Price: 19.990000 (6 decimals by default)
fmt.Printf("Price: %.2f\n", price)      // Price: 19.99 (2 decimals)

// %t - Boolean (true or false)
isValid := true
fmt.Printf("Valid: %t\n", isValid)      // Valid: true

// %v - Value (works with ANY type - your best friend!)
fmt.Printf("%v\n", 42)                  // 42
fmt.Printf("%v\n", "hello")             // hello
fmt.Printf("%v\n", true)                // true
fmt.Printf("%v\n", []int{1, 2, 3})      // [1 2 3]
fmt.Printf("%v\n", map[string]int{"a": 1})  // map[a:1]

content.title: When in Doubt, Use %v
content.message: If you're not sure which verb to use, %v almost always works. It automatically chooses the right format for any type. Use specific verbs like %d or %s when you need precise control over the output format.

content.text: Integer Format Verbs Explained
Beyond %d, Go offers verbs to print integers in different number systems. These are useful for bit manipulation problems or when debugging binary/hex values.
String and Character Verbs Explained
For strings and characters, you have a few options depending on whether you want plain output or quoted output (useful for debugging).
The %v Family: Universal Verbs for Any Type
The %v verb is incredibly versatile. It has three variants that give you different levels of detail, making them perfect for debugging.

items.label: %v
items.description: Default format. Prints the value in a sensible way. Works with any type.

items.label: %+v
items.description: For structs, adds field names. Shows {X:3 Y:4} instead of {3 4}.

items.label: %#v
items.description: Go-syntax representation. Shows the exact Go code to recreate the value.

items.label: %T
items.description: Type only. Prints the type of the value, not the value itself.

content.title: Debugging Strategy
content.message: Use %v for quick checks, %+v when debugging structs (to see field names), %#v when you need to recreate the exact value in code, and %T when you're unsure what type a variable is.

content.text: Floating Point Numbers
Floating point output needs careful formatting, especially when problems require specific decimal places.

content.code:
f := 3.14159265359

// Basic float verbs
fmt.Printf("%f\n", f)      // 3.141593      - default 6 decimal places
fmt.Printf("%e\n", f)      // 3.141593e+00  - scientific notation
fmt.Printf("%g\n", f)      // 3.14159265359 - compact representation

// Controlling decimal places
fmt.Printf("%.2f\n", f)    // 3.14          - 2 decimal places
fmt.Printf("%.4f\n", f)    // 3.1416        - 4 decimal places (rounds!)
fmt.Printf("%.0f\n", f)    // 3             - no decimal places

// Common interview pattern: print answer to N decimal places
answer := 2.0 / 3.0        // 0.6666...
fmt.Printf("%.6f\n", answer)  // 0.666667

content.text: Width and Padding
Sometimes you need to align output in columns or pad numbers with zeros. The width specifier controls the minimum field width.

content.code:
// Minimum width (right-aligned by default)
fmt.Printf("|%5d|\n", 42)      // |   42|  - width 5, right-aligned
fmt.Printf("|%-5d|\n", 42)     // |42   |  - width 5, left-aligned (- flag)
fmt.Printf("|%5s|\n", "hi")    // |   hi|  - works for strings too

// Zero padding (numbers only)
fmt.Printf("|%05d|\n", 42)     // |00042|  - pad with zeros
fmt.Printf("|%08d|\n", 42)     // |00000042|

// Combining width and precision for floats
f := 3.14159
fmt.Printf("|%8.2f|\n", f)     // |    3.14|  - width 8, 2 decimals
fmt.Printf("|%-8.2f|\n", f)    // |3.14    |  - left-aligned
fmt.Printf("|%08.2f|\n", f)    // |00003.14|  - zero-padded

content.text: Slices are Go's primary dynamic array type and the foundation of most algorithm solutions. Think of a slice as a flexible, resizable list that can grow or shrink as needed. Understanding their behavior is crucial for writing efficient code.
Arrays vs Slices: What's the Difference?

Go has two list-like types: arrays and slices. Arrays have a fixed size that cannot change, while slices can grow dynamically. In algorithm problems, you'll almost always use slices because input sizes vary.

content.code:
// Arrays: fixed size, cannot grow
var arr [5]int              // Creates [0 0 0 0 0]
arr := [3]int{1, 2, 3}      // Creates [1 2 3]

// Slices: dynamic size, can grow
s := []int{1, 2, 3}         // Creates a slice with values
s := make([]int, 5)         // Creates slice of length 5, all zeros
s := make([]int, 0, 10)     // Empty slice, but room for 10 items

content.title: Which One Should I Use?
content.message: Use []int{1, 2, 3} when you know the exact values. Use make([]int, 5) when you need 5 slots filled with zeros. Use make([]int, 0, 10) when you'll add items one by one but expect around 10 total.

content.text: Working with Slices

Every slice has two important properties: length (how many elements it currently holds) and capacity (how many elements it can hold before needing to reallocate memory). The append function adds elements to a slice and returns a new slice.
Adding Elements
The append function is how you add elements to a slice. It takes a slice and one or more values, and returns a new slice with those values added at the end.

content.title: Important
content.message: Always assign the result of append back to your slice variable: s = append(s, x). The append function may return a new slice if it needs more memory.

content.text: Slicing: Extracting Parts of a Slice
You can extract portions of a slice using the syntax s[start:end]. The start index is included, but the end index is excluded. This is called a half-open interval and is common in programming.

content.code:
s := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}

s[1:3]   // [2 3]     - from index 1 up to (not including) 3
s[:3]    // [1 2 3]   - first 3 elements (same as s[0:3])
s[2:]    // [3 4 5]   - from index 2 to the end
s[:]     // [1 2 3 4 5] - the entire slice

content.text: Copying Slices
When you slice a slice (like s[1:3]), you don't get a copy. Both slices point to the same underlying data, so changing one affects the other. Use the copy function when you need an independent copy.

content.time: O(1) access, O(1) amortized append, O(n) insert/delete
content.explanation: Accessing an element by index is instant. Appending is usually fast, but occasionally Go needs to allocate a bigger array and copy everything over.

content.text: 2D Slices for Grids and DP Tables
Many algorithm problems involve grids or tables (like dynamic programming). In Go, you create a 2D slice as a slice of slices. Each row must be allocated separately.
For DP tables that need a specific initial value (like -1 or infinity), you must set each element in a loop since Go only initializes to zero.
Removing Elements
Go doesn't have a built-in remove function. There are two common ways to remove an element: a fast way that changes the order, and a slower way that preserves order.
Reversing a Slice
To reverse a slice in place, swap elements from both ends moving toward the center.

content.title: Pre-allocate for Performance
content.message: When you know the final size, use make([]int, 0, n) to pre-allocate capacity. This avoids reallocations during append operations and can significantly speed up your solution.

content.text: Strings in Go are sequences of characters that cannot be changed after creation (they're immutable). This section covers how to work with strings effectively in algorithm problems.
What is a String?
A string is a sequence of bytes. For English text and most algorithm problems, each character is one byte. You can access individual characters by index, get the length, and extract substrings.

content.code:
s := "hello"

len(s)      // 5 - number of characters
s[0]        // 'h' - first character (as a byte)
s[len(s)-1] // 'o' - last character
s[1:4]      // "ell" - substring from index 1 to 3

content.text: Strings are Immutable

You cannot change a character inside a string directly. If you try s[0] = 'H', Go will give you an error. To modify a string, you need to convert it to a byte slice first, make your changes, then convert back.
Looping Through a String
There are two ways to loop through a string. Using a regular for loop gives you bytes (good for ASCII). Using range gives you runes (good for Unicode characters like emojis).

content.title: Which Loop Should I Use?
content.message: For most algorithm problems with English text, both loops work the same. Use the index loop (for i := 0...) when you need to access characters by position. Use range when you just need each character.

content.text: What are Runes?
A rune is Go's type for a single Unicode character. While English letters are 1 byte each, characters like emojis or Chinese characters can be 2-4 bytes. Runes handle this correctly.

content.code:
s := "Hello, 世界"  // Mix of English and Chinese

len(s)              // 13 - bytes, not characters!
len([]rune(s))      // 9 - actual character count

// Convert to rune slice for character-by-character work
chars := []rune(s)
chars[7]            // '世' - correct!
len(chars)          // 9 characters

content.title: When to Use Runes
content.message: For most algorithm problems, you won't need runes since inputs are usually ASCII. But if a problem mentions Unicode or special characters, convert to []rune first.

content.text: Useful String Functions
Go's strings package has many helpful functions. You need to import it with import "strings" at the top of your file.

content.code:
import "strings"

s := "Hello, World!"

// Checking content
strings.Contains(s, "World")   // true - does s contain "World"?
strings.HasPrefix(s, "Hello")  // true - does s start with "Hello"?
strings.HasSuffix(s, "!")      // true - does s end with "!"?

// Finding position
strings.Index(s, "o")          // 4 - position of first "o"
strings.LastIndex(s, "o")      // 8 - position of last "o"

content.text: Building Strings Efficiently
When you need to build a string piece by piece (like in a loop), don't use += because it creates a new string each time, which is slow. Use strings.Builder instead.
Character Math Trick
Characters in Go are just numbers. The letter 'a' is 97, 'b' is 98, and so on. You can do math with them, which is useful for counting letters or checking if something is a letter.

content.time: O(1) for access, O(n) for most operations
content.space: O(n) for conversions and new strings
content.explanation: Accessing a character by index is instant. Operations that create new strings (like ToLower or concatenation) take O(n) time where n is the string length.

content.text: A map (also called a hash map or dictionary) stores key-value pairs. You can quickly look up a value if you know its key. Maps are essential for counting items, finding duplicates, and solving problems like Two Sum.
What is a Map?
Think of a map like a real dictionary: you look up a word (the key) to find its definition (the value). In Go, you specify the types for both keys and values when creating a map.
Adding and Getting Values
Use square brackets to add or retrieve values. If you access a key that doesn't exist, Go returns the zero value (0 for int, "" for string, false for bool) instead of an error.

content.code:
m := make(map[string]int)

// Add a key-value pair
m["apple"] = 5
m["banana"] = 3

// Get a value
count := m["apple"]   // 5
count := m["orange"]  // 0 (key doesn't exist, returns zero value)

content.text: Checking if a Key Exists
Since missing keys return the zero value, how do you know if a key actually exists with value 0, or just doesn't exist? Go provides a second return value that tells you.

content.title: The Comma-OK Idiom
content.message: val, ok := m[key] is one of Go's most common patterns. The second value (ok) is true if the key exists, false otherwise. Use it whenever you need to distinguish between "key missing" and "key has zero value".

content.text: Deleting and Counting
Use the delete function to remove a key from a map. Use len to get the number of key-value pairs.

content.code:
m := map[string]int{"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3}

len(m)         // 3 - number of keys

delete(m, "b") // Remove key "b"

len(m)         // 2 - now only "a" and "c" remain

content.text: Looping Through a Map
Use range to loop through all key-value pairs in a map. You can also loop through just the keys by ignoring the value.

content.title: Map Order is Random
content.message: Maps in Go have no guaranteed order. Each time you loop through a map, the keys may come in a different order. If you need a specific order, collect the keys into a slice and sort it first.

content.text: Pattern: Counting Frequency
One of the most common uses of maps in algorithms is counting how many times each item appears. Since missing keys return 0, you can simply increment without checking if the key exists.
Pattern: Using Map as a Set
Go doesn't have a built-in Set type, but you can use a map with bool values to track which items you've seen. This is useful for finding duplicates or checking membership.
Pattern: Two Sum
The classic Two Sum problem asks: find two numbers in an array that add up to a target. Using a map, you can solve this in one pass by storing each number and checking if its complement exists.
Using Structs as Keys
You can use structs as map keys, which is useful for grid problems where you need to track visited coordinates. The struct must contain only comparable types (no slices or maps).

content.time: O(1) average for add, get, delete, and check
content.space: O(n) where n is number of key-value pairs
content.explanation: Maps use hashing to provide near-instant lookups regardless of size. This is why they're so useful for algorithm problems.

content.text: A set is a collection of unique items with no duplicates. Unlike slices, sets let you quickly check if an item exists. Go doesn't have a built-in Set type, but you can easily create one using a map.
What is a Set?

Sets are useful when you need to track unique items, check membership, or remove duplicates. The key operations are: add an item, check if an item exists, and remove an item. All of these should be fast.
Creating a Set with map[T]bool
The simplest way to create a set in Go is using a map where the keys are your items and the values are always true. This makes the syntax clean and readable.
Common Set Operations
Here are all the basic operations you can do with a set. They all work in O(1) time on average.
Example: Remove Duplicates from a Slice
A common use case for sets is removing duplicate values from a slice while preserving the order of first appearance.
Set Operations: Union and Intersection
Sometimes you need to combine sets or find common elements. Union gives you all items from both sets. Intersection gives you only items that appear in both sets.
Memory-Efficient Set (Advanced)
For very large sets, you can save memory by using struct{} as the value type instead of bool. An empty struct uses zero bytes, while bool uses 1 byte per entry. The syntax is slightly more awkward.

content.title: Which Should I Use?
content.message: Use map[int]bool for algorithm problems. It's cleaner and the memory difference rarely matters. Use map[int]struct{} only when storing millions of items or in production systems where memory is critical.

content.time: O(1) average for add, remove, and check
content.space: O(n) where n is number of items
content.explanation: Sets built on maps inherit the same fast O(1) operations. This makes them ideal for tracking seen items or checking membership in algorithm problems.

content.text: A stack is a data structure where you can only add and remove items from one end, called the top. Think of a stack of plates: you can only take the top plate off, and you can only add a new plate on top. This is called Last-In-First-Out (LIFO).
What is a Stack?
Stacks have three main operations: push (add to top), pop (remove from top), and peek (look at top without removing). Go doesn't have a built-in stack type, but slices work perfectly for this.
Creating a Stack
Use an empty slice as your stack. The end of the slice is the "top" of the stack.
Push: Adding to the Stack
To push an item onto the stack, use append. The new item becomes the top of the stack.

content.code:
stack := []int{}

stack = append(stack, 1)  // stack: [1]
stack = append(stack, 2)  // stack: [1, 2]
stack = append(stack, 3)  // stack: [1, 2, 3] <- 3 is on top

content.text: Pop: Removing from the Stack
To pop an item, first get the top element, then shrink the slice by one. Always check if the stack is empty before popping to avoid errors.
Peek: Looking at the Top
Sometimes you need to see the top element without removing it. This is called peeking.
Complete Stack Operations
Here's a summary of all stack operations in one place.

content.title: Common Pattern
content.message: Always check len(stack) > 0 before peeking or popping. Accessing an empty slice will cause a runtime panic.

content.text: Example: Valid Parentheses

One of the most classic stack problems: given a string of brackets, check if every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket in the correct order. Push opening brackets onto the stack, and when you see a closing bracket, check if it matches the top.
Example: Reverse a String Using Stack
Stacks naturally reverse order. Push all characters, then pop them all.
When to Use a Stack
Stacks are useful for problems involving matching pairs, reversing order, tracking history (like undo), and processing nested structures. Common patterns include:

items.description: Push opening, pop and match closing

items.label: Reversing
items.description: Push all, then pop all

items.label: Expression evaluation
items.description: Track operators and operands

items.label: Undo operations
items.description: Push actions, pop to undo

items.label: DFS traversal
items.description: Iterative depth-first search

content.time: O(1) for push, pop, and peek
content.space: O(n) where n is number of elements
content.explanation: All stack operations are constant time. Push uses amortized O(1) because Go's slice may occasionally need to grow, but this averages out.

content.text: A queue is like a line at a store: the first person in line is the first to be served. This is called First-In-First-Out (FIFO). Queues are essential for breadth-first search (BFS) and processing things in order.
What is a Queue?

Unlike stacks where you add and remove from the same end, queues add at the back and remove from the front. The main operations are: enqueue (add to back), dequeue (remove from front), and peek (look at front).
Creating a Queue
Go doesn't have a built-in queue, but slices work well. The front of the slice is the front of the queue, and we add to the back.
Enqueue: Adding to the Queue
To add an item to the queue, use append. New items go to the back and wait their turn.
Dequeue: Removing from the Queue
To remove an item, get the front element and then slice off the first element. Always check if the queue is empty first.
Peek: Looking at the Front
Sometimes you need to see who's at the front without removing them.
Complete Queue Operations
Here's a summary of all queue operations.

content.title: Memory Note
content.message: When you slice queue[1:], Go doesn't release the memory of the removed element. For algorithm problems this is fine, but for long-running programs with millions of operations, consider using a circular buffer.

content.text: Example: BFS with a Queue

Breadth-first search (BFS) explores all neighbors at the current level before moving to the next level. This requires a queue to process nodes in order. Here's a simple example of level-order tree traversal.
What is a Deque?
A deque (double-ended queue, pronounced "deck") allows adding and removing from both ends. It's like a queue where you can also cut in line at the front or leave from the back.
Deque Operations
With a deque you can push/pop from both front and back. Here's how to implement basic deque operations using a slice.

content.title: When to Use Each
content.message: Use a queue for BFS, processing in order, or any FIFO scenario. Use a deque when you need to add/remove from both ends, like in sliding window problems or certain cache implementations.

content.text: When to Use Queues
Queues appear in many algorithm problems. Here are the common patterns:

items.label: BFS traversal
items.description: Explore level by level in trees and graphs

items.label: Level-order traversal
items.description: Process tree nodes level by level

items.label: Shortest path (unweighted)
items.description: BFS finds shortest path in unweighted graphs

items.label: Task scheduling
items.description: Process tasks in the order they arrived

items.label: Sliding window
items.description: Deque helps track min/max in a window

content.space: O(n) where n is number of elements
content.explanation: Enqueue (append) is O(1) amortized. Dequeue (slice[1:]) is O(1) but doesn't free memory. For most algorithm problems, this implementation is efficient enough.

content.text: A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node contains a value and a pointer to the next node. Unlike arrays/slices where elements are stored together in memory, linked list nodes can be scattered anywhere, connected only by these pointers.
What is a Linked List?

Think of a linked list like a treasure hunt: each clue (node) tells you where to find the next clue. You must follow the chain from the beginning (head) to find any element. This makes access slower than arrays, but insertions and deletions are faster.
The ListNode Structure
In Go, we define a linked list node as a struct with two fields: Val (the data) and Next (a pointer to the next node). The last node's Next is nil, marking the end of the list.
Creating a Linked List
To create a linked list, you create nodes and connect them. The & operator gives you a pointer to the node.
Traversing a Linked List
To visit every node, start at the head and follow the Next pointers until you reach nil. Use a temporary variable so you don't lose the head.
The Dummy Head Trick

Many linked list problems have tricky edge cases: what if the head itself needs to be removed? The dummy head pattern solves this by creating a fake node that points to the real head. This way, even if the head changes, we can return dummy.Next.

content.title: When to Use Dummy Head
content.message: Use a dummy head whenever the head of the list might change during your operation, like when removing nodes, merging lists, or inserting at the beginning.

content.text: Fast and Slow Pointers

A powerful technique for linked lists is using two pointers that move at different speeds. The slow pointer moves one step at a time, while the fast pointer moves two steps. This helps find the middle of a list or detect cycles.
Detecting a Cycle
If a linked list has a cycle (the last node points back to an earlier node), the fast pointer will eventually catch up to the slow pointer. If there's no cycle, the fast pointer will reach nil.
Reversing a Linked List

Reversing a linked list is a classic interview problem. The idea is to change each node's Next pointer to point to the previous node instead of the next one. You need three pointers: prev (starts as nil), curr (current node), and next (to save the next node before we change the link).
Common Linked List Patterns
Here are the most common patterns you'll encounter in linked list problems:

items.description: Simplifies edge cases when head might change

items.label: Fast/slow pointers
items.description: Find middle, detect cycles, find nth from end

items.label: Reverse
items.description: Reverse entire list or a portion

items.label: Merge
items.description: Combine two sorted lists into one

items.label: Two pointers (same speed)
items.description: Keep one pointer n steps behind another

content.title: Common Mistakes
content.message: Always check for nil before accessing node.Next to avoid panics. When modifying links, save the next node first or you'll lose the rest of the list.

content.time: O(n) for traversal, O(1) for insert/delete at known position
content.space: O(1) for most operations, O(n) for recursion
content.explanation: You must traverse to find a node (O(n)), but once found, inserting or deleting is O(1) since you just change pointers. Compare this to arrays where finding is O(1) but inserting is O(n).

content.text: A tree is a hierarchical data structure where each node can have children. Unlike linked lists which are linear, trees branch out. Binary trees are a special case where each node has at most two children, called left and right.
What is a Tree?

Think of a family tree or a file system. There's a root at the top, and it branches down. Key terms: the root is the topmost node, a leaf is a node with no children, and the height is the longest path from root to leaf.
The TreeNode Structure
In Go, we represent a binary tree node with a struct containing a value and pointers to left and right children. If a child doesn't exist, the pointer is nil.
Creating a Binary Tree
To build a tree, create nodes and connect them through the Left and Right pointers.
Tree Traversal: Visiting Every Node
There are different orders to visit all nodes in a tree. The three main depth-first traversals differ only in when you process the current node relative to its children.

items.label: Inorder
items.description: Left, then Root, then Right. Gives sorted order for BST.

items.label: Preorder
items.description: Root, then Left, then Right. Good for copying a tree.

items.label: Postorder
items.description: Left, then Right, then Root. Good for deleting a tree.

content.text: Inorder Traversal (Left, Root, Right)
Inorder visits the left subtree first, then the current node, then the right subtree. For a binary search tree, this gives nodes in sorted order.
Preorder Traversal (Root, Left, Right)
Preorder visits the current node first, then the left subtree, then the right subtree. This is useful when you need to process a node before its children.
Level Order Traversal (BFS)
Level order visits nodes level by level, from top to bottom and left to right. This uses a queue (BFS) instead of recursion.
Finding the Maximum Depth

The maximum depth (or height) of a tree is the number of nodes on the longest path from root to leaf. This is a classic recursive problem: the depth is 1 plus the maximum of the left and right subtree depths.
Checking if Two Trees are the Same
To check if two trees are identical, compare their values and recursively check both subtrees. Base case: two nil nodes are equal, but one nil and one non-nil are not.
Common Tree Patterns
Most tree problems follow a few common patterns:

items.label: Recursive DFS
items.description: Solve for left and right subtrees, combine results

items.label: BFS with queue
items.description: Process level by level, good for level-based problems

items.label: Pass info down
items.description: Pass values from parent to children via parameters

items.label: Return info up
items.description: Return values from children to parent via return values

content.title: Tree Problem Approach
content.message: For most tree problems, ask: Can I solve this by combining solutions from the left and right subtrees? If yes, use recursion. If you need to process level by level, use BFS with a queue.

content.space: O(h) for recursion, O(n) for BFS queue
content.explanation: All traversals visit each node exactly once. Recursive solutions use O(h) stack space where h is the tree height. For a balanced tree h = log(n), for a skewed tree h = n.

content.text: A heap is a special tree-based data structure that keeps track of the minimum (or maximum) element efficiently. It's perfect for problems where you repeatedly need to find and remove the smallest or largest item, like priority queues or finding the top K elements.
What is a Heap?

Think of a heap like a tournament bracket. In a min heap, the smallest element is always at the top (the champion). When you remove it, the heap reorganizes to put the next smallest at the top. This makes finding the minimum O(1) and removing it O(log n).

items.label: Min Heap
items.description: Smallest element is always at the top

items.label: Max Heap
items.description: Largest element is always at the top

items.label: Priority Queue
items.description: A common use of heaps where items are processed by priority

content.text: Go's container/heap Package
Go doesn't have a built-in heap type. Instead, it provides a container/heap package that works with any type you define. You need to implement 5 methods to tell Go how your heap should behave.
Creating a Min Heap
Here's a complete min heap for integers. The key is the Less function: using < makes it a min heap (smallest on top). Copy this as a template for your own heaps.
Using the Heap
Once you've defined your heap type, use the heap package functions to work with it. Important: always use heap.Push and heap.Pop, not the methods directly.

content.title: Important
content.message: Always call heap.Init() before using a heap. Always use heap.Push() and heap.Pop(), not the Push/Pop methods directly. The direct methods don't maintain the heap property.

content.text: Creating a Max Heap
To make a max heap (largest on top), simply flip the comparison in the Less function. Change < to >.
Example: Find K Largest Elements

A classic heap problem: find the K largest elements from an array. The trick is to use a min heap of size K. As you scan through, keep only the K largest seen so far. The smallest of those K will be at the top, ready to be replaced if you find something larger.
When to Use a Heap
Heaps are the right choice when you need to repeatedly find the minimum or maximum element. Common patterns include:

items.label: Top K / Bottom K
items.description: Find K largest or smallest elements

items.label: Kth largest element
items.description: Find the element at position K when sorted

items.label: Merge K sorted lists
items.description: Always pick the smallest head

items.label: Running median
items.description: Use two heaps: max heap + min heap

items.label: Task scheduling
items.description: Process highest priority first

content.title: Top K Trick
content.message: For 'top K largest', use a MIN heap of size K. For 'top K smallest', use a MAX heap of size K. This seems backwards but it works: you keep removing the worst of your K candidates.

content.time: O(log n) for push/pop, O(1) for peek, O(n) for init
content.explanation: Adding or removing an element requires reorganizing the heap, which takes O(log n). Looking at the top element is O(1). Building a heap from scratch with Init() is O(n).

content.text: A graph is a data structure that represents connections between things. It consists of vertices (nodes) and edges (connections). Graphs are everywhere: social networks (people connected by friendships), maps (cities connected by roads), and even mazes (cells connected to adjacent cells).
What is a Graph?

Think of a graph like a subway map. Each station is a vertex, and each line connecting stations is an edge. Some lines are one-way (directed graph), others go both ways (undirected graph). Some connections might have different costs like travel time (weighted graph).

items.label: Directed Graph
items.description: Edges have direction: A→B doesn't mean B→A (like Twitter follows)

items.label: Undirected Graph
items.description: Edges go both ways: A—B means you can go A→B and B→A (like Facebook friends)

items.label: Weighted Graph
items.description: Edges have values: the cost, distance, or time to traverse

items.label: Unweighted Graph
items.description: All edges are equal, no associated values

content.text: How to Represent a Graph

The most common way to represent a graph is an adjacency list: for each vertex, store a list of its neighbors. In Go, we use either a slice of slices (for numbered vertices) or a map (for any vertex type).
Adjacency List with Slice (Numbered Vertices)
When vertices are numbered 0 to n-1, use a slice of slices. Each index represents a vertex, and the slice at that index contains its neighbors. This is the most common format in coding problems.
Adjacency List with Map (Any Vertex Type)
When vertices are strings, structs, or not numbered sequentially, use a map. The key is the vertex, and the value is a slice of neighbors.
Weighted Graph
For weighted graphs, store both the neighbor and the weight. Define a struct for edges, or use a pair of values.
Graph Traversal: DFS vs BFS
There are two main ways to explore all vertices in a graph. Understanding when to use each is crucial for solving graph problems.

items.label: DFS (Depth-First)
items.description: Go as deep as possible, then backtrack. Uses recursion or stack. Good for: finding paths, detecting cycles, exploring all possibilities.

items.label: BFS (Breadth-First)
items.description: Explore all neighbors first, then their neighbors. Uses queue. Good for: shortest path (unweighted), level-order traversal.

content.text: DFS (Depth-First Search)

DFS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. Think of it like exploring a maze: you keep going until you hit a dead end, then backtrack and try another path. The key is to track visited nodes to avoid infinite loops.

content.title: DFS Pattern
content.message: The DFS pattern is always: (1) check if visited, (2) mark as visited, (3) process current node, (4) recurse on neighbors. The visited map prevents infinite loops in cyclic graphs.

content.text: BFS (Breadth-First Search)

BFS explores all nodes at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on. This makes it perfect for finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs. Think of it like ripples in a pond: you explore outward in layers.
BFS for Shortest Path

To find the shortest path between two nodes in an unweighted graph, use BFS and track the distance. Since BFS explores layer by layer, the first time you reach the target is guaranteed to be the shortest path.

content.title: BFS Shortest Path Only Works for Unweighted Graphs
content.message: BFS finds shortest path only when all edges have equal weight. For weighted graphs, use Dijkstra's algorithm (with a min heap) instead.

content.text: Grids as Graphs

A 2D grid is just a graph in disguise! Each cell is a vertex, and adjacent cells (up, down, left, right) are connected by edges. You don't need to build an explicit adjacency list. Just use the grid directly and calculate neighbors with direction arrays.
Example: Number of Islands

A classic grid problem: count connected groups of '1's (land) in a grid of '1's and '0's (water). Each island is a connected component. Use DFS to explore and mark each island, incrementing the count each time you find an unvisited '1'.
When to Use DFS vs BFS

items.label: Use DFS for
items.description: Finding any path, detecting cycles, topological sort, exploring all possibilities, connected components

items.label: Use BFS for
items.description: Shortest path (unweighted), level-order traversal, finding nearest, spreading/infection problems

content.title: Graph Problem Recognition
content.message: If you see words like 'connected', 'path', 'reachable', 'adjacent', 'neighbor', or a grid, think graph! Build an adjacency list (or use the grid directly) and apply DFS/BFS.

content.time: O(V + E) for DFS/BFS where V = vertices, E = edges
content.space: O(V) for visited set + O(V) for recursion stack (DFS) or queue (BFS)
content.explanation: Both DFS and BFS visit each vertex once and examine each edge once. For a grid with m×n cells, V = m×n and E = O(m×n) since each cell has at most 4 neighbors.

content.text: Sorting is one of the most common operations in programming. Go's sort package makes it easy to sort slices of any type. You'll use sorting constantly: to prepare data for binary search, to group similar items together, or as a first step in many algorithms.
Why Sorting Matters
Many problems become much easier once data is sorted. For example, finding duplicates, searching efficiently, or solving two-sum problems. Sorting is often the first step in an optimal solution.

items.label: Unsorted search
items.description: O(n) - must check every element

items.label: Sorted + binary search
items.description: O(log n) - eliminate half each step

items.label: Finding duplicates unsorted
items.description: O(n^2) or O(n) with extra space

items.label: Finding duplicates sorted
items.description: O(n) - duplicates are adjacent

content.text: Built-in Sorting Functions
Go provides convenience functions for sorting slices of common types. These sort in-place (modify the original slice) and sort in ascending order by default.
Check if Already Sorted
Sometimes you need to verify if data is sorted before processing. Go provides functions to check without modifying the slice.
Reverse (Descending) Sort
To sort in descending order (largest first), wrap your slice type with sort.Reverse. This flips the comparison logic.

content.title: IntSlice vs []int
content.message: sort.IntSlice is a type that implements sort.Interface. You need it for sort.Sort() and sort.Reverse(). For simple ascending sort, just use sort.Ints() directly.

content.text: Custom Sorting with sort.Slice
The real power comes from custom sorting. sort.Slice lets you define exactly how to compare elements. You provide a "less" function that returns true if element i should come before element j.
Sorting 2D Slices (Intervals)
A common pattern is sorting intervals or pairs. You can sort by the first element, second element, or any combination. This is essential for interval merging, scheduling, and meeting room problems.
Sorting Structs
When working with structs, sort.Slice lets you sort by any field. This is useful for sorting objects by priority, timestamp, score, etc.
Stable Sort

A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal elements. Use sort.SliceStable when the original order matters for ties. For example, sorting by age while keeping alphabetical order for people with the same age.
Binary Search with sort.Search

Once data is sorted, you can search in O(log n) time using binary search. Go's sort.Search finds the first index where a condition becomes true. Think of it as finding the "boundary" in a sorted array.
Check if Element Exists
To check if a specific value exists in a sorted slice, find where it should be and verify it's actually there.

content.title: sort.Search Requires Sorted Data
content.message: Binary search only works on sorted slices. The condition function must be monotonic: it returns false for indices 0..k-1 and true for indices k..n-1. If the condition is never true, sort.Search returns len(slice).

items.description: Two Sum, 3Sum, container with most water

items.label: Sort by start
items.description: Merge intervals, insert interval

items.label: Sort by end
items.description: Greedy scheduling, non-overlapping intervals

items.label: Sort + Binary Search
items.description: Find target, count occurrences, search insert position

items.label: Custom comparator
items.description: Largest number, sort by frequency

content.time: O(n log n) for sorting, O(log n) for binary search
content.explanation: Go uses pdqsort (pattern-defeating quicksort), a hybrid algorithm that's O(n log n) worst case. Binary search halves the search space each step, giving O(log n).

content.text: Two pointers is a technique where you use two index variables to traverse a data structure. Instead of using nested loops (O(n^2)), two pointers often let you solve problems in a single pass (O(n)). It's one of the most common patterns in coding interviews.
When to Use Two Pointers

Two pointers work well when you need to find pairs, compare elements from different positions, or partition/rearrange arrays. The key insight is that moving pointers strategically eliminates possibilities without checking every combination.

items.label: Opposite Direction
items.description: Start at both ends, move toward middle (sorted arrays, palindromes)

items.label: Same Direction
items.description: Both start at beginning, fast/slow pattern (remove duplicates, partition)

items.label: Fixed Gap
items.description: Maintain fixed distance between pointers (sliding window variant)

content.text: Pattern 1: Opposite Direction (Converging Pointers)

Start with one pointer at the beginning and one at the end. Move them toward each other based on some condition. This works great for sorted arrays because you can decide which pointer to move based on whether the current sum/comparison is too small or too large.
Example: Two Sum in Sorted Array

Given a sorted array, find two numbers that add up to a target. The brute force approach checks all pairs in O(n^2). With two pointers, we can do it in O(n): if the sum is too small, move the left pointer right (to get a larger number); if too large, move the right pointer left.
Example: Valid Palindrome
Check if a string reads the same forwards and backwards. Compare characters from both ends moving inward. If any pair doesn't match, it's not a palindrome.
Example: Container With Most Water

Given heights of vertical lines, find two lines that form a container holding the most water. The area is limited by the shorter line. Start with the widest container (both ends), then try to find taller lines by moving the shorter pointer inward.

content.title: Why Move the Shorter Line?
content.message: Moving the taller line can only decrease or maintain the height (still limited by shorter line) while decreasing width. Moving the shorter line might find a taller line, potentially increasing the area despite smaller width.

content.text: Pattern 2: Same Direction (Fast/Slow Pointers)

Both pointers start at the beginning. The 'fast' pointer scans through all elements, while the 'slow' pointer marks where to write or tracks a boundary. This is perfect for in-place array modifications.
Example: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
Given a sorted array, remove duplicates in-place and return the new length. The slow pointer tracks where the next unique element should go. The fast pointer scans for unique elements.
Example: Move Zeroes to End
Move all zeroes to the end while maintaining the relative order of non-zero elements. The slow pointer marks where the next non-zero should go. Swap non-zeroes to the front.
Example: Remove Element
Remove all occurrences of a value in-place. Similar to move zeroes, but we're removing a specific value.
Pattern 3: Three Pointers (3Sum)

For problems involving three elements (like 3Sum), fix one element with a regular loop and use two pointers on the remaining array. This reduces O(n^3) brute force to O(n^2). The array must be sorted first.

content.title: Handling Duplicates in 3Sum
content.message: The tricky part of 3Sum is avoiding duplicate triplets. After finding a valid triplet, skip over duplicate values for both left and right pointers. Also skip duplicates for the outer loop variable i.

content.title: Two Pointer Template
content.message: For opposite direction: left, right := 0, len(arr)-1; for left < right { ... }. For same direction: slow := 0; for fast := 0; fast < len(arr); fast++ { if condition { slow++ } }.

content.time: O(n) for two pointers, O(n^2) for 3Sum
content.explanation: Two pointers traverse the array once (or converge from ends). Each pointer moves at most n times, so total is O(n). 3Sum has an outer loop O(n) times two pointers O(n), giving O(n^2).

content.text: Sliding window is a technique for processing contiguous sequences (subarrays or substrings) efficiently. Instead of recalculating everything from scratch for each position, you 'slide' a window across the data, updating only what changes. This reduces many O(n^2) or O(n*k) problems to O(n).
What is a Sliding Window?

Imagine looking through a window at a row of houses. You can only see a few houses at a time. As you walk down the street, the window 'slides': a new house enters your view on one side, and another leaves on the other side. You never go back to recount houses you've already passed.

items.label: Fixed Window
items.description: Window size stays constant (e.g., max sum of k consecutive elements)

items.label: Variable Window
items.description: Window grows/shrinks based on conditions (e.g., smallest subarray with sum >= target)

items.label: With HashMap
items.description: Track character frequencies inside window (e.g., longest substring without repeats)

content.text: Pattern 1: Fixed Size Window
When the window size k is fixed, initialize with the first k elements, then slide by adding the new element and removing the oldest. This avoids recalculating the entire window each time.
Example: Maximum Sum of Subarray of Size K

Find the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays of exactly size k. Brute force would sum k elements for each starting position: O(n*k). With sliding window, we maintain a running sum and update it in O(1) for each slide.

content.title: Fixed Window Template
content.message: Initialize: sum first k elements. Slide: for i := k; i < n; i++ { add nums[i], remove nums[i-k], update result }. The window always contains elements from i-k+1 to i.

content.text: Pattern 2: Variable Size Window (Shrinkable)

When finding the smallest or largest window satisfying a condition, use two pointers: 'right' expands the window, 'left' shrinks it. Expand until the condition is met, then shrink while still valid to find the minimum.
Example: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
Find the smallest contiguous subarray with sum >= target. Expand the window until sum reaches target, then shrink from the left to find the minimum length while still valid.
Pattern 3: Sliding Window with HashMap
For substring problems involving character frequencies or uniqueness, combine sliding window with a hashmap. The map tracks what's inside the current window, making it easy to check validity.
Example: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
Find the length of the longest substring with all unique characters. Use a map to track the last position of each character. When you see a repeat, jump the left pointer past the previous occurrence.

content.title: Check if Character is in Current Window
content.message: When checking for repeats, verify the previous occurrence is within the current window (idx >= left). Characters outside the window don't cause conflicts.

content.text: Example: Minimum Window Substring (Hard)

Find the smallest substring of s that contains all characters of t (including duplicates). This combines variable window with character frequency counting. Expand until all characters are covered, then shrink to minimize.
When to Use Sliding Window

Look for keywords like 'contiguous', 'substring', 'subarray', 'consecutive', 'window of size k', 'minimum/maximum length'. If the problem asks about contiguous elements with some constraint, sliding window is likely the approach.

items.label: Fixed window
items.description: Max/min/average of every k elements, string anagrams

items.label: Shrinkable (find min)
items.description: Smallest subarray with sum >= k, minimum window substring

items.label: Expandable (find max)
items.description: Longest substring with at most k distinct chars, max consecutive ones

items.label: With frequency map
items.description: Anagram search, permutation in string, all unique characters

content.title: Variable Window Template
content.message: for right := 0; right < n; right++ { add nums[right] to window; for window is invalid OR (for min problems) window is valid { remove nums[left]; left++ } update result }. For max length: update result after inner loop. For min length: update result inside inner loop.

content.time: O(n) - each element enters and leaves window at most once
content.space: O(1) for fixed window, O(k) for hashmap where k is character set size
content.explanation: The right pointer visits each element once. The left pointer also moves at most n times total (never backwards). So total operations are O(2n) = O(n), not O(n^2).

content.text: Backtracking is a systematic way to explore all possible solutions by building them incrementally. When you hit a dead end (a choice that can't lead to a valid solution), you 'backtrack' by undoing the last choice and trying a different path. It's like exploring a maze: go forward until you hit a wall, then go back and try another direction.
When to Use Backtracking

Backtracking is ideal when you need to find all solutions (or one solution) that satisfy certain constraints. Common problems include generating combinations, permutations, subsets, solving puzzles, and constraint satisfaction problems.

items.label: Subsets/Combinations
items.description: Choose which elements to include (order doesn't matter)

items.label: Permutations
items.description: Arrange elements in different orders (order matters)

items.label: Constraint Satisfaction
items.description: Find arrangements that satisfy rules (N-Queens, Sudoku)

items.label: Path Finding
items.description: Find all paths in a graph or grid

content.text: The Backtracking Template

Every backtracking solution follows the same pattern: (1) Choose an option, (2) Explore by recursing, (3) Unchoose (undo) to try the next option. In Go, we typically define the recursive function as a closure so it can access the result slice and current state.

content.title: Critical: Always Copy Slices Before Saving
content.message: When saving a solution, use append([]int{}, current...) to make a copy. If you just append current directly, all saved solutions will share the same underlying array and get corrupted as you backtrack. This is the #1 backtracking bug in Go.

content.text: Example 1: Generate All Subsets

Generate all possible subsets (the power set) of a given array. For each element, we have two choices: include it or skip it. Every intermediate state is a valid subset, so we save at every step, not just at leaves.
Example 2: Generate Combinations
Generate all combinations of k elements from n elements. This is like subsets, but we only save when we have exactly k elements. We stop exploring branches that can't possibly reach k elements.

content.title: Pruning Optimization
content.message: Pruning means cutting off branches early when you know they can't lead to valid solutions. In combinations, if you need 3 more elements but only 2 remain, there's no point exploring further. Good pruning can dramatically speed up backtracking.

content.text: Example 3: Generate Permutations

Generate all orderings (permutations) of elements. Unlike subsets where order doesn't matter, permutations care about order: [1,2] and [2,1] are different. We use a 'used' array to track which elements are already in the current permutation.
Subsets vs Permutations: Key Difference

items.label: Subsets
items.description: Use 'start' parameter, loop from start to end. Each element considered once. [1,2] same as [2,1].

items.label: Permutations
items.description: Use 'used' array, loop from 0 every time. Same elements, different orders. [1,2] different from [2,1].

content.text: Example 4: N-Queens (Constraint Satisfaction)

Place N queens on an N×N chessboard so no two queens attack each other (same row, column, or diagonal). This is a classic constraint satisfaction problem. We place one queen per row and backtrack when we can't place a queen safely.

content.title: Diagonal Trick
content.message: For \ diagonals, all cells have the same (row - col) value. For / diagonals, all cells have the same (row + col) value. Store these in maps to check diagonal attacks in O(1).

items.description: Generate all 2^n subsets

items.description: Find combinations that sum to target

content.space: O(n) for recursion stack + O(result size) for storing solutions
content.explanation: Backtracking explores exponential or factorial solution spaces. The time complexity is often unavoidable because you need to generate all solutions. However, good pruning can eliminate large portions of the search tree and dramatically improve average case performance.

content.text: Dynamic Programming (DP) is a technique for solving problems by breaking them into smaller overlapping subproblems and storing the results to avoid redundant computation. Instead of solving the same subproblem multiple times, you solve it once and remember the answer. This transforms exponential-time solutions into polynomial time.
When to Use Dynamic Programming

DP is applicable when a problem has two properties: (1) Optimal substructure, meaning the optimal solution can be built from optimal solutions to subproblems, and (2) Overlapping subproblems, meaning the same subproblems are solved multiple times. Common signals include 'minimum/maximum', 'count ways', 'is it possible', and recursive solutions with repeated work.

items.label: Memoization (Top-Down)
items.description: Start with the main problem, recurse into subproblems, cache results

items.label: Tabulation (Bottom-Up)
items.description: Start with smallest subproblems, build up to the answer iteratively

content.text: The Problem with Plain Recursion

Consider the Fibonacci sequence: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2). A naive recursive solution recalculates the same values exponentially many times. fib(5) calls fib(3) twice, fib(2) three times, and so on. For fib(40), this takes billions of operations.
Approach 1: Memoization (Top-Down DP)

Memoization adds caching to recursion. Before computing a subproblem, check if you've already solved it. If yes, return the cached result. If no, compute it, cache it, then return. This is the easiest way to convert a recursive solution to DP.

content.title: Map vs Slice for Memoization
content.message: Use a map when keys are sparse or non-integer. Use a slice when keys are dense integers 0 to n, as slice access is faster. Initialize slice values to -1 or another invalid value to distinguish 'not computed' from 'computed as 0'.

content.text: Approach 2: Tabulation (Bottom-Up DP)

Tabulation builds the solution iteratively from the smallest subproblems up. Create a table (usually an array), fill in base cases, then fill remaining cells in order so each cell's dependencies are already computed. No recursion needed.
Space Optimization
Often you don't need the entire table, just the most recent values. For Fibonacci, each value only depends on the previous two, so we only need two variables instead of an array of n elements.
Example: Coin Change (Classic 1D DP)

Given coin denominations and a target amount, find the minimum number of coins needed. For each amount, try using each coin and take the minimum. This is unbounded knapsack: you can use each coin unlimited times.
Example: Longest Common Subsequence (2D DP)

Find the length of the longest subsequence present in both strings. A subsequence maintains relative order but doesn't need to be contiguous. Use a 2D table where dp[i][j] represents the LCS of the first i characters of text1 and first j characters of text2.
Space-Optimized 2D DP
When each row only depends on the previous row, you can reduce O(m*n) space to O(n) by keeping only two rows. Alternate between them as you iterate.
The 5-Step DP Strategy
When facing a DP problem, follow these steps systematically:

content.text: Go slices are incredibly powerful but have some tricky behaviors. Mastering these idioms will help you write cleaner, more efficient algorithm code and avoid common bugs. This section covers essential slice operations you'll use constantly in coding problems.
Understanding Slice Internals

A slice is a view into an underlying array. It has three components: a pointer to the array, a length (how many elements you can access), and a capacity (how many elements the array can hold). Multiple slices can share the same underlying array, which is both powerful and dangerous.

content.code:
// Slice header: (pointer, length, capacity)
arr := [5]int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}  // Array
s := arr[1:4]                  // Slice: [2, 3, 4]

fmt.Println(len(s))  // 3 (elements 2, 3, 4)
fmt.Println(cap(s))  // 4 (can grow to include 5)

// Slices share underlying array!
s[0] = 99
fmt.Println(arr)  // [1, 99, 3, 4, 5] - arr changed too!

content.title: Slice Aliasing Bug
content.message: When you slice a slice (s2 := s1[1:3]), both share the same underlying array. Modifying one affects the other. This is the #1 source of slice bugs. When in doubt, make a copy.

content.text: Copying Slices

To create an independent copy that doesn't share the underlying array, use one of these methods. This is essential for backtracking, storing intermediate results, or any time you need to modify a slice without affecting the original.
Deep Copy of 2D Slices
For 2D slices (slice of slices), a shallow copy only copies the outer slice. The inner slices still point to the same arrays. You must copy each inner slice individually.
Insert Element at Index
Go doesn't have a built-in insert function. Use append with slicing to insert an element at any position. This is O(n) because elements must shift.
Delete Element at Index
There are two ways to delete: preserving order (O(n), shifts elements) or not preserving order (O(1), swaps with last element). Choose based on whether order matters.

content.title: O(1) Delete for Sets
content.message: When using a slice as a set (order doesn't matter), always use the O(1) delete. This is common in problems where you need to remove elements efficiently.

content.text: Filter In-Place

Remove elements that don't match a condition without allocating a new slice. Use a write pointer to track where to place kept elements. This is the same technique as 'remove duplicates' or 'move zeroes'.
Reverse a Slice
Reverse elements in-place using two pointers from opposite ends. This is useful for many problems including rotating arrays, palindrome checks, and reversing words.
Rotate Array
Rotate an array by k positions to the right. The trick is to use three reverses: reverse all, reverse first k, reverse rest. This is O(n) time and O(1) space.
Pre-allocate for Performance
When you know (or can estimate) the final size, pre-allocate capacity to avoid repeated reallocations during append. Each reallocation copies all elements to a new array.
Common Slice Patterns Summary

content.message: Use make([]T, 0, capacity) when building results incrementally. Use make([]T, length) when you'll assign to indices directly. The difference: length 0 means you must append; length n means you have n zero values ready to overwrite.

content.text: Many coding problems require sorting by custom criteria: sort by multiple fields, sort without modifying the original, or sort in unusual ways. Go's sort.Slice makes custom sorting easy with a comparison function. Master these patterns to handle any sorting requirement.
How sort.Slice Works

sort.Slice takes a slice and a 'less' function. The less function receives two indices i and j and returns true if the element at i should come before the element at j. Think of it as answering: 'Is element i less than element j?'
Multi-Key Sorting

Often you need to sort by one field, then by another field when the first is equal. Check the primary field first; if they differ, return the comparison. If they're equal, fall through to the secondary comparison.

content.title: Multi-Key Pattern
content.message: For N-key sorting: check field 1, return if different. Check field 2, return if different. ... Check field N, return result. Each 'if different, return' handles one level of sorting.

content.text: Sorting Without Modifying Original

Sometimes you need the sorted order but can't modify the original slice. Create an array of indices [0, 1, 2, ...] and sort the indices based on the values they point to. This gives you a 'ranking' of elements.
Sorting Pairs/Tuples Together
When you have parallel arrays (like values and their frequencies), you often need to sort one while keeping the other aligned. Either combine them into a struct, or sort indices.
Custom String Sorting: Largest Number

A classic problem: arrange numbers to form the largest possible number. The trick is comparing concatenations: should '3' come before '30'? Compare '330' vs '303'. Since '330' > '303', '3' should come first.
Stable Sort

A stable sort preserves the original order of equal elements. Use sort.SliceStable when ties should maintain their input order. This is important when you've already sorted by one criterion and want to sort by another without disrupting the first sort.
Sort by Frequency
A common problem pattern: sort elements by how often they appear. First count frequencies with a map, then sort using those counts.

content.title: Less Function Must Be Consistent
content.message: The less function must define a strict ordering: if less(i,j) is true, then less(j,i) must be false. If both are equal, both should return false. Inconsistent comparisons cause undefined behavior or infinite loops.

content.text: Go 1.18 introduced generics (type parameters), allowing you to write functions and data structures that work with any type. Instead of writing separate functions for []int, []string, []float64, you write one generic function that works with all of them. This makes your algorithm helpers reusable and type-safe.
What Are Generics?

Generics let you write code that works with multiple types without losing type safety. The type is specified when you use the function, not when you write it. Think of it as a template: you define the logic once, and Go fills in the actual type when needed.
Type Constraints

Type parameters have constraints that specify what operations are allowed. The most common constraints are 'any' (any type), 'comparable' (types that support == and !=), and 'cmp.Ordered' (types that support <, >, <=, >=).

items.description: Any type at all. Can only assign, pass to functions, or use in interfaces.

items.label: comparable
items.description: Types that support == and !=. Includes all basic types, pointers, channels, arrays, structs with comparable fields.

items.label: cmp.Ordered
items.description: Types that support ordering operators (<, >, etc.). Includes integers, floats, and strings.

content.text: Even experienced Go developers make these mistakes in algorithm problems. Understanding why they happen will help you avoid them in interviews and write more robust code.
1. Slice Reference Sharing (The #1 Backtracking Bug)

This is the most common bug in backtracking problems. In Go, slices are references to an underlying array. When you append a slice to your results, you're storing a reference, not a copy. As the slice changes during backtracking, all your stored "results" change too!
The fix is to make a copy of the slice before storing it. The idiom `append([]int{}, current...)` creates a new slice and copies all elements into it.

content.title: Memory Trick
content.message: Whenever you store a slice in backtracking, ask yourself: "Am I storing a reference or a copy?" If in doubt, copy with `append([]T{}, slice...)`.

content.text: 2. Map Iteration Order is Random

Go deliberately randomizes map iteration order to prevent code from depending on it. If your algorithm needs consistent ordering (e.g., generating all permutations, comparing outputs), you must sort the keys first.
3. Integer Overflow in Binary Search

The classic mid-point calculation `(left + right) / 2` can overflow if both values are large. This is a famous bug that existed in Java's binary search implementation for years. The safe formula is `left + (right - left) / 2`.
For other arithmetic operations, check for overflow before it happens:
4. Nil Slice vs Empty Slice
A nil slice and an empty slice behave the same for most operations (both have len 0, both can be appended to), but they're different values. This matters when comparing with nil or encoding to JSON.
In interviews, prefer nil slices (simpler to declare). Mention you'd use empty slices if the API requires non-null JSON arrays.
5. Modifying Slice During Iteration

Removing elements from a slice while iterating forward causes bugs: you either skip elements or get index-out-of-range errors. The range loop captures the original length, but your deletions change the slice.
There are two safe approaches: iterate backwards (so deletions don't affect remaining indices), or build a new slice.
6. String Indexing Returns Bytes, Not Characters

In Go, strings are byte sequences. Indexing a string with `s[i]` returns a byte (uint8), not a character (rune). For ASCII text, bytes and characters are the same. For Unicode text (emoji, Chinese, etc.), a single character can be multiple bytes.

content.code:
s := "hello"
fmt.Printf("%T %c\n", s[0], s[0])  // uint8 h

// ASCII: bytes work fine
if s[0] == 'h' { fmt.Println("Starts with h") }  // Works

// Unicode: bytes don't work!
s := "hello" // " is a 3-byte character
fmt.Println(len(s))  // 8 (5 letters + 3 bytes for ")
fmt.Println(s[5])    // 226 (first byte of ", not the character!)

content.title: Interview Tip
content.message: Most algorithm problems use ASCII strings, so byte indexing is fine. But mention to the interviewer that you'd handle Unicode differently in production. It shows awareness.

content.text: 7. Forgetting to Handle Edge Cases
Many interview failures come from missing edge cases, not wrong algorithms. Train yourself to always check these cases before diving into the main logic.
